analysis.one_liner: Makes large drug makers with recent federal fraud settlements help fund NIH and FDA medical research.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: it was referred to the Senate Health Committee on January 29, 2015 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Big drug companies that paid $1 million or more to settle federal fraud or misconduct cases in the past five years, and that made over $1 billion in net income, would owe the government 1% of net income for each blockbuster drug (over $1 billion in annual sales) that was developed using federally funded research. The money would go to the FDA and NIH for medical research, and a company that refused to pay could not sell its unpaid blockbuster drugs at all.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and patients. NIH and FDA research budgets would get new money raised from companies rather than from general taxes, with priority uses including radical-innovation research, diseases that drive federal health spending (Medicare, Medicaid, VA), and early-career scientists. The public would also get a published list of which manufacturers paid and how much.

how_it_helps.text: Payments are split between FDA and NIH and targeted at research on diseases that disproportionately drive federal health care spending, unmet medical needs, and fundamental science that doesn't pay off quickly [S2][S3].
The bill funds early-career scientists through research grants and training programs, addressing the difficulty new researchers face winning NIH support [S3].

HHS must publish, in the Federal Register, which manufacturers paid, which blockbuster drugs triggered the payments, and the amounts — public accountability for companies that settled misconduct cases [S2][S3].
Enforcement is automatic: a company's unpaid blockbuster drug is deemed misbranded and cannot legally be sold until the payment is made [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large brand-name drug manufacturers — specifically those with $1 billion or more in net income and a recent settlement with a federal agency over fraud or other violations. The levy multiplies by each covered blockbuster drug, so companies with many billion-dollar drugs built on federally funded science would owe the most.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big drug makers with fraud settlements

drawbacks.text: The trigger is narrow: only companies that settled federal misconduct cases pay, so the burden falls on a handful of large firms each year rather than spreading across the industry — and the amounts could fluctuate sharply depending on which settlements occurred in a five-year window [S3].

The definition of a 'covered blockbuster drug' is sweeping — any billion-dollar drug whose patent relates to federally funded science counts — so manufacturers would face open-ended liability that is hard to predict or plan for [S3].
The collection mechanism is blunt: declaring a drug misbranded and pulling it from the market until payment could interrupt patient access to medicines as a collection tactic [S2][S3].
Payments only flow if FDA and NIH appropriations do not fall from the prior year, so the money supplements but never backfills budget cuts [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill channels real new money into medical research and does it on the theory that companies that defrauded federal health programs, and profited from publicly funded science, should help pay for the next round of it. The honest costs are predictability and collateral risk: the drug-by-drug multiplier and the threat of pulling medicines off the market make the levy hard for companies to budget, and a misapplied 'misbranded' designation could affect patients. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much weight one gives to conditioning market access on settling past misconduct.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee — chaired by a Republican — never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on January 29, 2015, joined by Democratic colleagues Sen. Cardin, Sen. Brown, and Sen. Baldwin [S3][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S1][S5].
No further action of any kind appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee or floor vote [S5].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill received no vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large drug manufacturers that had settled federal fraud cases kept the money the bill would have assessed — roughly 1% of net income per blockbuster drug — and NIH and FDA never received the supplemental research funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large drug manufacturers that settled fraud cases

for.name: 4 Democratic Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all listed cosponsors were Democrats, including Sens. Cardin, Brown, and Baldwin.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill saw no committee action in two years.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; no floor vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat (five senators total), the Republican-chaired committee never acted, and no vote was ever held on the bill [S3][S4][S5].

industries.note: Companies with $1 billion-plus net income and recent federal fraud or misconduct settlements would owe 1% of net income for each blockbuster drug developed with federally funded research, with nonpayment making the drug unsellable. The industry's interest in defeating the bill ran directly against the research funding the public would have gained.

The payments would have been split between FDA and NIH in proportion to their discretionary funding, adding money for regulatory science, radical-innovation research, and early-career scientists — capacity that benefits patients and the research workforce directly.
